newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senator Thurmond poised for record 8th term.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senator Thurmond poised for record 8th term.

text.p: Republican Strom Thurmond, the oldest U.S. senator ever, looks poised to win a record eighth term next week despite some South Carolina voters' concerns about his mental agility at 93.
Thurmond's 41 years in the Senate fall just two years shy of the life of his Democratic opponent, Elliott Close, whom Thurmond has continuously dubbed too inexperienced.

"This race is a simple choice for the voters between an experienced conservative and a liberal who has no experience," Thurmond said at a fundraiser recently. "I think I can do more in six years than he can do in 60 years," he told supporters ahead of the Nov. 5 election.
Thurmond, who if re-elected would become the longest-serving senator ever next May, plans spending the final days of his re-election campaign crossing the state to meet as many voters as possible.

Campaigning last week on what has become known as the "Thurmond-ator Tour '96," the World War II hero regarded as something of a legend in South Carolina appealed to voters to give him one last term. "If you elect me again it will be the last time I run," he told supporters at a weekend rally.
Thurmond turns 94 in December and if re-elected would be 100 when his term ends.
The most recent Charleston Post and Courier newspaper poll shows Thurmond leading Close 50 percent to 40 percent. The poll has a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points.

Close, 43, a real estate magnate who is also heir to the textiles fortune of Springs Industries in Fort Mill, has never held an elected office. A political newcomer, Close won the endorsement of one of South Carolina's largest newspapers when the Greenville News gave him lukewarm support on Sunday.

"Close is inexperienced and not well known, but he is an authentic citizen office-seeker worthy of election on his merits," the newspaper said in an editorial. It said it did not back Thurmond this time based on concerns about his mental agility as well as his refusal to debate Close.
The State newspaper gave lukewarm support to Thurmond despite its criticism of the senior senator for refusing to step aside so a younger Republican could run for the seat.

On the stump, Thurmond tells supporters that he can still function and argues the race is about clout, not age. "Because of my experience, I think I'm in more of a position to help you than somebody who has never held an office," he said.

Some Democrats and political analysts say experience aside Close missed the opportunity to unseat Thurmond by running a weak campaign. "Somehow I don't think he has caught on," University of South Carolina political science professor Blease Graham said.

Another criticism is that Close does not mix well with the electorate. "If people shake your hand, they're more likely to vote for you than not, so you've got to do some of that," Close said. "(But) I'll never be an overtly gregarious hand-pumping politician. That's not my style."
